edges.description: Reproduces progressive spinal motor neuron loss and limb paralysis on a defined genetic cause.
edges.limitations: Disease is driven by supraphysiological transgene copy number rather than by a single endogenous heterozygous allele, so onset and tempo are set partly by expression level. The model captures the SOD1 arm of ALS specifically and does not reproduce the TDP-43 proteinopathy that defines most human ALS, which is a fidelity limit for ALS generally but is arguably appropriate for ALS1 in particular. The expression level is not a neutral scaling factor: the standard high-expressing line is resistant to prion-like seeding that readily accelerates disease in a low-expressing sub-line, so this model actively conceals the propagation arm.

edges.description: Loss of SOD1 function does not cause the motor neuron degeneration seen in ALS1, constraining the mechanism to a gain of function.
edges.limitations: A null allele is not the human genotype: ALS1 patients are heterozygous for a missense allele and retain expressed protein, so the model tests only whether absence of dismutase activity is sufficient. It cannot address whether a partial loss of activity contributes alongside the toxic gain of function, and the enhanced vulnerability after axonal injury shows SOD1 is not functionally dispensable under stress.

edges.description: Cell-type-restricted removal of the mutant gene isolates the glial contribution to the progression phase.
edges.limitations: Excision efficiency is incomplete and lineage-specific Cre drivers are not perfectly restricted, so residual mutant expression in the targeted lineage limits how cleanly the contributions can be attributed. As with all SOD1 transgenics, the finding is established for SOD1-driven disease and does not establish the same division of labour in TDP-43-driven ALS.

edges.description: Elevated NfL reports ongoing axonal degeneration. It falls with SOD1 lowering and rises before phenoconversion in presymptomatic carriers, which is what makes it usable as both a pharmacodynamic and a treatment-timing marker.

nodes.description: Misfolded SOD1 accumulates as ubiquitin-positive cytoplasmic inclusions in motor neurons and glia. These inclusions are the pathological signature that separates ALS1 from the rest of ALS: they are immunoreactive for ubiquitin but not for TDP-43, and biochemically detectable pathological TDP-43 species are absent. Because TDP-43 proteinopathy is present in the great majority of sporadic and non-SOD1 familial ALS, SOD1-mutant cases sit outside that pathological class, and results obtained in SOD1 systems cannot be assumed to transfer to TDP-43-driven ALS.

nodes.description: Misfolded SOD1 binds the ERAD component Derlin-1, impairing retrotranslocation of misfolded substrates out of the endoplasmic reticulum. The resulting ER stress activates apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 (ASK1) and a death pathway downstream of it. Deleting ASK1 extends survival in SOD1-mutant mice without removing the mutant protein, so this arm contributes to motor neuron loss through a route that does not require lowering SOD1 itself. That experiment measured neuron loss and lifespan and did not measure aggregation, so it does not establish that this arm is independent of the aggregation arm.

nodes.description: Vulnerable alpha motor neurons do not pass straight from health to death. Longitudinal single-nucleus profiling of the SOD1-G93A mouse defines an intermediate transcriptional and chromatin state, termed the disease-associated motor neuron (DM) state, that precedes cell death and is driven by an identifiable transcription-factor network. Two things make it more than a mouse descriptor: forcing those factors up in human motor neurons induces DM features, and the signature is conserved in human ALS spinal cord. It is placed downstream of the toxic arms and upstream of degeneration because that is where the profiling places it; the specific arms that drive the transition are not resolved.

nodes.description: The central mechanistic claim of ALS1. Variant SOD1 adopts a non-native conformation that is toxic in its own right, and this toxicity is independent of the loss of dismutase activity. Three independent lines of evidence converge: mice completely lacking SOD1 have normal motor neurons and no motor deficits; the Asp90Ala allele causes ALS while leaving erythrocyte dismutase activity essentially normal; and a transgene encoding Gly93Ala — a substitution with little effect on enzyme activity — is sufficient to paralyse mice. Loss of dismutase function is therefore neither necessary nor sufficient for the disease, and SOD1 lowering rather than SOD1 replacement is the rational therapeutic direction.

nodes.description: ALS1 is not a cell-autonomous motor neuron disease. Using mice in which the mutant gene can be excised in selected lineages, mutant SOD1 acting within motor neurons was shown to set disease onset and the early phase of progression, while mutant SOD1 within microglia and astrocytes governs the later, rapid phase. Onset and progression are therefore distinct phases driven by different cell types, which is why glia-directed therapy is a rational target for slowing established disease even though it would not be expected to delay onset.

nodes.description: Misfolded SOD1 templates the misfolding of native SOD1, and the resulting species move between cells, so pathology spreads rather than arising independently at each site. This is the mechanistic candidate for the contiguous, focal-to-generalized anatomical spread that characterises ALS clinically. Release from motor neurons is at least partly active, occurring through P2X7 receptor activation, and material taken up by recipient neurons and microglia reproduces disease-relevant responses — ER stress in neurons and TNF-alpha release from microglia. The glial response is drawn as an edge below. The ER stress seen in recipient neurons is reported in a cell model and is not the Derlin-1-dependent mechanism curated as a separate node here, so no edge is drawn between this arm and that one.

nodes.description: Intrathecally administered antisense oligonucleotide that directs RNase H-mediated degradation of SOD1 mRNA, lowering synthesis of both wild-type and variant SOD1 protein. It is the first therapy directed at the ALS1 mechanism itself rather than at downstream neuroprotection. The evidence has a specific shape that should not be smoothed over: the pivotal phase 3 VALOR trial met its biomarker endpoints — CSF SOD1 and plasma neurofilament light both fell — but missed its primary clinical endpoint at 28 weeks, and regulatory approval rested on the neurofilament biomarker rather than on a demonstrated functional benefit. Signals favouring earlier over delayed initiation emerged in the open-label extension and strengthened with longer follow-up: the final integrated VALOR/OLE analysis, with 3.5 years or more of follow-up, reported numerically less decline in function, respiratory capacity, strength and quality of life in the early-start group, and survival longer than the expected natural history. Those comparisons remain non-randomized after week 28, so the durable evidence for clinical benefit is a within-trial early-versus-delayed contrast rather than a placebo-controlled one. Post-approval case series report stabilisation and are uncontrolled.
